title: Values in Both Lists
oneLiner: Return the values that appear in both lists, once each, in the order they first appear in the first list.
keyTakeaway: Turn the list you search into a set first: then each "is it in there?" check is O(1) and the whole job is O(n + m) instead of O(n · m). A second set stops the same value being output twice.
explanation:
Given two lists of whole numbers, return the values that appear in both. Each value appears in the output once, in the order of its first appearance in the first list: ([2, 1, 2, 3], [3, 2, 2]) gives [2, 3].

The direct approach loops over the first list and searches the second for each value: with n and m items that's n × m comparisons. Instead, put the second list into a set once (new HashSet<int>(b) in C#, set(b) in Python), then walk the first list and keep a value if it's in that set and you haven't output it yet (a second set, as in Remove Duplicates). Building the set costs O(m) and the walk O(n), so the whole thing is O(n + m).

Set intersection (IntersectWith, &) finds the common values too, but loses the order the tests ask for, so you still need the walk over the first list.
